data.title: Enmarket to Open Newest Eatery Location in Rincon, GA
data.description:
WORCESTER, MA / ACCESS Newswire / November 20, 2026 / Nouria, a family-owned convenience, food, and fuel retailer serving New England and the Southeast, will hold the Grand Opening of its newest Eatery location in its Rincon, GA Enmarket store at 6188 Highway 21 South, on Monday, November 23rd. The Eatery is Enmarket's proprietary fresh food concept inside select Enmarket convenience stores.

The Eatery is known for fresh prepared foods, especially Southern comfort-food like fried chicken and specialty hot side dishes. In addition, the Eatery offers fresh-cracked-egg breakfast sandwiches, hearty subs, savory pizza, and other delicious options prepared with convenience and quality in mind. Guests will be able to sample several of these items on the 23rd. Special Grand Opening offers include two slices of pepperoni or cheese pizza and a large fountain drink for $4, and a chicken sandwich, potato wedges, and large fountain drink for $4.99. Both specials are available through December 20th.

"We are excited to bring The Eatery to our Rincon location so guests can enjoy our delicious fresh food and have another reason to visit us here," said Joy Almekies, director of fresh food and culinary at Nouria. "We want our guests to think of Enmarket when it comes to delicious, fresh food in addition to being convenient place to stop for on-the-go items."

About Nouria

Nouria is a family-owned convenience, food, and fuel retail company headquartered in Worcester, Massachusetts. Founded in 1989 by Tony El-Nemr, the company operates more than 300 convenience store locations, 93 car washes, and multiple travel centers across New England and the Southeast. Nouria also supplies fuel to independent retail sites under brands including Shell, Irving, Gulf, Sunoco, and Citgo. The company is committed to delivering an outstanding guest experience and supporting the communities it serves.

Media Contact

David Heilbronner, Director of Marketing | dheilbronner@nouria.com | 508-314-5149

data.title: Is Social Security a Ponzi scheme? No. Don't get carried away with 1930s-era prophecies of doom.
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

Wisconsin Republican Sen. Ron Johnson called Social Security a 'scam' and urged lawmakers to shut it down

Social Security is not a Ponzi scheme. A Ponzi scheme is born of fraud and relies on a constant stream of new unwitting investors.

Fear can lead us to do and say unexpected things.

It can push us toward panic selling, drive us to make wild assumptions about the world, and sometimes force us to take a hard look at our own finances. We are especially prone to these impulses when we are looking for something or someone to blame.

Wisconsin Republican Sen. Ron Johnson, the chairman of the Committee on the Budget, on Wednesday took aim at Social Security ahead of a hearing on the subject, calling it a scam. "It's grotesque and at this point, there really is no way to fix Social Security," he said. "It is a Ponzi scheme."

Social Security is not a Ponzi scheme. A Ponzi scheme is born of fraud and relies on a stream of new unwitting investors who pay the returns promised to earlier ones. Social Security is a pay-as-you-go program established by federal law, in which payroll taxes fund benefits.

He isn't the only one who's frustrated with Social Security. Experts attribute an expected shortfall in Social Security to demographic factors - older workers retiring, with some claiming benefits early out of fear that the funds will run out.

Social Security is a pay-as-you-go program established by federal law.

Unless Congress acts, the combined trust funds will run out in 2034, covering just 83% of benefits. A new AARP report said: "The share of gross domestic product subject to Social Security's payroll tax, the program's primary income source, has fallen steadily over the past four decades."

The Social Security taxable maximum is $184,500 for 2026 and $192,300 for 2027, meaning earnings above those limits are not subject to Social Security payroll taxes. In other words, a growing share of national income is excluded, contributing to the expected shortfall in funds.

Like Johnson, a Moneyist reader also used the "P" word. "The thought of living to 100 terrifies me more than dying. For me, the biggest fraud is telling people to wait until 70 to retire just to maximize their Social Security benefits - as if that's the only factor worth considering."

They continued: "I grew up in the 1980s, and the advice to never count on Social Security is sounding more and more like a warning than a prediction. I fear there will be a run on Social Security similar to the bank runs before the Great Depression. Long live the Ponzi!"

Don't miss: Is $1 million enough for a household to retire? The answer keeps changing.

Addressing the criticisms

The reader is essentially asking four questions: (1) Will fear trigger a Social Security crisis? (2) Is Social Security a Ponzi scheme? (3) Why sacrifice your 60s to get a bigger check at 70? And (4) Can you really count on Social Security?

(1) As for fear leading to a crisis: Probably not, so do not get carried away with 1930s-era prophecies of doom and gloom. A run on a bank involves a large number of people withdrawing their money and, if the bank cannot meet those withdrawals, even an otherwise solvent institution can fail.

I grew up in the 1980s too, and here's a fun fact about Generation X: The American Institute of Stress says we are apparently more stressed out than other generations. The main reason for that, researchers theorize, is that we are worried about falling short on our retirement goals.

(2) Social Security is a social-insurance program funded by workers and employers to provide support in retirement, prevent vulnerable people from falling into poverty and provide economic stability during downturns. It is at risk of a shortfall in funding, not annihilation.

Social Security is at risk of a shortfall in funding, not annihilation.

(3) You can claim Social Security at 62, but doing so reduces your monthly benefit by 30% compared with waiting until your full retirement age (FRA) of 67. Waiting until 70 increases your benefit by 8% for each year you delay beyond 67. That's 24% more in total.

If you are collecting Social Security and remain below FRA throughout 2026, you can earn up to $24,480 before benefits are withheld. Above that limit, $1 is withheld for every $2 you earn. At FRA, Social Security recalculates your benefit to account for withholdings.

Yes, some people do claim Social Security benefits early due to fears about the program's long-term viability. But the program values stability, security and peace of mind over recklessness, madcap investments and promises of riches.

(4) You can count on Social Security, which is not projected to disappear. Payroll taxes and other incoming revenue will keep funding benefits. Under current projections, though, that revenue would cover only 83% of scheduled benefits from the combined trust funds in 2034.

Don't miss: 'I still have horrible memories of the Bernie Madoff scandal': At 63, who can I trust with my $655K retirement fund?

Why we have Social Security

Social Security was created in 1935 in response to the Great Depression and was not intended to maximize investment returns. Today, it provides a social safety net against the financial hardships of retirement, disability and the loss of a family's breadwinner.

There are two separate funds: the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund and the Disability Insurance Trust Fund. Their reserves are invested in special-issue U.S. Treasury securities, backed by the full faith and credit of the federal government.

So what about this looming funding crisis? The Congressional Budget Office said earlier this year that the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, which pays retirement and survivors benefits, is projected to run out of reserves in 2032.

The Bipartisan Policy Center, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, said in a June report that, at that point, incoming revenue would cover just 78% of scheduled benefits from that fund. Without congressional action, those shortfalls would mean across-the-board reductions in benefits.

There is already a demographic 'run' on Social Security.

"The program's long-run outlook worsened significantly this year," it said. "The Social Security Administration (SSA) revised its fertility and immigration projections downward." The 75-year shortfall has risen to approximately $30 trillion - up from $26 trillion last year.

There is already a demographic "run" on Social Security. The Bipartisan Policy Center said "an aging population is a major contributor to the problem." The ratio of workers to beneficiaries has dropped from 5-to-1 in 1960 to 2.6-to-1 in 2025 and is projected to fall to 1.9-to-1 by 2075.

The Social Security Disability Insurance Trust Fund is projected to remain solvent until 2100, the end of the Board of Trustees' 75-year projection period, but the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, under current estimates, won't have enough to pay full benefits in 2032.

We are encouraged to delay our dream life, save more, work longer and maximize our retirement contributions. Still, the price of financial security should not be spending our 60s worrying about our 70s, 80s and 90s, and beyond. For millions of people, however, that worry is a daily reality.

Keep calm and carry on working, if you can, and saving for retirement.

Related: Should wealthier Americans forgo their Social Security benefits as a charitable gesture?

Check out The Moneyist's private Facebook group, where members help answer life's thorniest money issues. Post your questions, weigh in on the latest Moneyist columns or email The Moneyist at qfottrell@marketwatch.com.

'It feels like he's quietly building a separate life': My husband inherited $500,000, but he refuses to spend it on our home

-Quentin Fottrell

data.title: Anthropic's stock slides closer to IPO price and drags down the AI trade
data.description:
By Emily Bary

Anthropic's inability to hold its opening stock price has been seen as 'bad for the rest of tech'

Anthropic finished with a $1.29 trillion valuation on Thursday.

There was no honeymoon period for Anthropic after its record-breaking initial public offering.

Shares of the AI company are down more than 14% in midday action on Friday, making for a gloomy second day of trading. Anthropic's stock (ANT) is at $83.21, well below its $111.50 opening price, and falling closer to its $83 IPO price.

It's a downbeat sign for the broader technology ecosystem as well, with AI stocks taking a beating across the board. Among notable losers are shares of Sandisk (SNDK), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Dell Technologies (DELL), Nebius Group (NBIS) and Arm Holdings (ARM).

"The vast majority of this continued selling pressure in the last 24 hours feels more to do with" the Anthropic IPO than it does with some less-than-perfect earnings reports in the technology sector, according to Jefferies trading-desk analyst Jeffrey Favuzza.

He wrote in a note to clients that Anthropic's inability to hold its opening price and the downward pressure in Friday's premarket action is being viewed as "bad for the rest of tech."

Anthropic's IPO was seen as a tentpole event for the AI trade. The company finished with a $1.29 trillion valuation on Thursday, according to Dow Jones Market Data. Friday's action brings that down to $1.09 trillion.

"Anthropic's strong debut alongside a falling technology sector suggests investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth," David Miller, the chief investment officer at Catalyst Funds, said in emailed comments.

Some analysts initiated coverage of Anthropic's stock after Thursday's close, chiming in with mixed views.

Don't miss: After Anthropic's 'bittersweet' IPO, here's what lies ahead

"We are cautious, not negative," wrote Seaport Research's Jay Goldberg, who launched coverage of shares with a neutral rating.

He called Anthropic an "incredible company," but also one "asking for an incredible leap of faith by investors."

"We think the company will need time to grow into its valuation and answer some very big questions about its growth trajectory," he continued. For instance, the company saw 43% revenue growth from the second quarter to the third quarter. That compared with a much faster 144% growth rate from the first quarter to the second quarter.

Goldberg referred to that as a "worrying" deceleration. "To merit its valuation, it will need to see much higher growth rates over the next two years," he added.

William Blair's Arjun Bhatia was more upbeat, calling Anthropic a "generational company driving a generational technology shift" as he began his own coverage of the stock with an outperform rating.

"Questions about the future are worth asking, even those that don't have an answer at this point," he wrote.

But at the same time, he and his team "don't want to miss the forest for the trees."

"We think AI is a generational shift in the tech landscape, and Anthropic is leading the charge in developing AI with a select handful of other companies," Bhatia wrote. "Over the next decade, we think Anthropic is only going to become more important and consume a greater portion of enterprise spend," meaning it will command more of the budget that businesses have to allocate toward technology.

See also: Anthropic soared in its debut as stocks tanked. Only one other IPO has done that since 1990.

-Emily Bary

data.title: Why year-end portfolio rebalancing is a risky bet that bonds will beat stocks in 2027
data.description:
By Mark Hulbert

Portfolio rebalancing involves many implicit bets that investors may not even be aware of

Investors should be aware of all of the active bets they're making when regularly rebalancing their portfolios.

Will bonds beat stocks in 2027?

It's an urgent question, since between now and the end of the year your financial adviser may be placing a bet with your portfolio that they will. And chances are good that neither your adviser nor you will even be aware of that bet.

That's because many, if not most, advisers rebalance their clients' portfolios near the end of the year. That involves selling those portions of your portfolio that have been the better year-to-date performers and using the proceeds to buy more of the underperformers. Many, if not most, investors consider rebalancing to be as uncontroversial as buying and holding an index fund.

Actually, however, annual rebalancing involves a number of very specific bets about the relative returns of the various asset classes you own. One of those bets is that a given year's better-performing asset will be a poorer performer the subsequent year, and vice versa. Currently, since stocks have outperformed bonds so far this year, rebalancing now is an implicit bet that bonds will outperform stocks in 2027.

This year-to-year reversal is often not the case. Consider the 135 calendar years since 1793 in which stocks outperformed long-term Treasury bonds. (I relied on the database constructed by Edward McQuarrie, a professor emeritus at the Leavey School of Business at Santa Clara University in California.) In 77 of the immediately subsequent calendar years, stocks also outperformed Treasuries - 57% of the time, in other words.

The assumptions of rebalancing

It's important to be aware of all of the active bets you're making when regularly rebalancing your portfolios. There are at least three:

-- After being an above-average performer, each of your asset classes needs to have an above-average chance of performing poorly.

-- This reversal tendency must consistently repeat at the same interval as your rebalancing frequency. If you're an annual rebalancer, for example, then stocks' performance relative to bonds should also reverse at the annual frequency. Even if stocks and bonds regularly reverse their relative returns, annual rebalancing would still do you no good if they reverse themselves at different frequencies.

-- Finally, each of your portfolio's assets must follow the same reversal frequency. If stocks' relative returns reverse at one frequency, but bonds at another, annual rebalancing will be only randomly profitable.

To be sure, you will have to rebalance eventually, when your asset classes' actual portfolio weights deviate too far from their assigned weights. But that may be a lot less frequently than you think. There have been a number of periods since 1793, each lasting more than 10 years, in which the stock allocation of an un-rebalanced 60% stock/40% bond portfolio never deviated by more than five percentage points from the 60% default.

These are some of the reasons why the late John Bogle, the founder of the Vanguard Group, classified as "noise" the long-term difference in returns between an annually rebalanced portfolio and one which does so less often. "Rebalancing [annually] is a personal choice, not a choice that statistics can validate," Bogle once wrote in his "Ask Jack" blog. "There's certainly nothing the matter with doing it... but also no reason to slavishly worry about" it.

Mark Hulbert is a regular contributor to MarketWatch. His Hulbert Ratings tracks investment newsletters that pay a flat fee to be audited. He can be reached at mark@hulbertratings.com

-Mark Hulbert

data.title: ExchangeRight Takes First Fast-Track DST Full Cycle
data.description:
ExchangeRight Takes First Fast-Track DST Full Cycle

ExchangeRight, one of the nation’s leading providers of diversified DST and REIT investments, has announced that it has completed its 35th full-cycle event with the successful acquisition of Essential Income 2 DST’s portfolio by ExchangeRight’s Essential Income REIT. This full-cycle event marks the first completed exit of an offering from ExchangeRight’s REIT Fast-Track series, which is structured to provide investors with stable monthly income during a targeted two-year hold period, followed by accelerated, tax-deferred access to the Essential Income REIT’s Operating Partnership via Section 721 exchange.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261120604958/en/

As of September 30, 2026, the Essential Income REIT is invested in a diversified portfolio of 475 properties across 39 states with net leases backed by 44 historically recession-resilient and primarily investment-grade tenants.

In connection with closing, ExchangeRight facilitated the tax-deferred 721 exchange into the Essential Income REIT’s Operating Partnership, protecting 100% of investor capital and generating total net annual investor returns of 6.01%. The exit provides pro rata access to the REIT’s monthly income, broader diversification, increased growth potential, enhanced liquidity, and estate planning advantages.

As of September 30, 2026, the Essential Income REIT is invested in a diversified portfolio of 475 properties across 39 states with net leases backed by 44 historically recession-resilient and primarily investment-grade tenants. The REIT has never reduced or missed its monthly dividend and has fully covered its dividend with Adjusted Funds From Operations (“AFFO”) since its inception, representing its ability to fully fund its cash distributions solely from its operations instead of from investor equity or financing. The REIT’s AFFO-to-distribution coverage ratio is 102.92% from inception through September 30, 2026.

“We are thrilled to take our first Essential Income DST offering full cycle as part of our aggregation strategy, illustrating how our DST and REIT investment solutions are designed to work together for the benefit of investors,” said Joshua Ungerecht, a managing partner at ExchangeRight. “This full-cycle event protected 100% of DST investor capital and income and has provided access to the tax-advantaged income, increased depreciation benefits, potential liquidity, long-term growth potential, and estate planning benefits of the Essential Income REIT. At the same time, this exit was designed to contribute high-quality net-leased properties to the REIT, further diversifying its portfolio and enhancing the REIT’s credit profile and net asset value.”

This milestone extends ExchangeRight’s track record to 35 full-cycle events, all of which have protected 100% of investor capital upon exit. All of the company’s past and current offerings have met or exceeded projections since inception and ExchangeRight’s 35 full-cycle offerings have generated an average annual total return of 8.53%. Past performance of ExchangeRight and its offerings does not guarantee future results. “Investment-grade” refers to tenants whose long-term corporate debt rating is considered investment grade by Standard & Poor’s, Moody’s, and/or Fitch.

About ExchangeRight

ExchangeRight and its affiliates’ vertically integrated platform features more than $8.1 billion in assets under management that are diversified across over 1,400 properties and 33 million square feet throughout 47 states, as of October 31, 2026. ExchangeRight pursues its passion to empower people to be secure, free, and generous through 1031 DST portfolios, Essential Income REIT, and cash management funds, all of which have historically met or exceeded investor projections since ExchangeRight’s inception. On behalf of investors nationwide, the company structures and manages net-leased portfolios of assets backed primarily by investment-grade corporations that have successfully operated in the industrial, necessity retail, and healthcare industries. Past performance does not guarantee future results. Please visit www.exchangeright.com for more information.

data.title: Pernod Ricard: Annual Combined Shareholders’ Meeting of 20 November 2026
data.description:
Pernod Ricard: Annual Combined Shareholders’ Meeting of 20 November 2026

Regulatory News:

Press Release – Paris, 20th November 2026, 5:30 PM

Pernod Ricard (Paris:RI) held its Annual Combined Shareholders’ Meeting today (the “Shareholders’ Meeting”), chaired by Alexandre Ricard, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, notably to approve the parent company and the consolidated financial statements for the fiscal year ended 30 June 2026.

All the resolutions were adopted, including:

  • Approval of the parent company financial statements and of the consolidated financial statements for the fiscal year ended 30 June 2026.
  • Annual dividend: €4.70 per share. As an interim dividend of €2.35 per share was paid on 24 July 2026, the balance of €2.35 per share will be detached on 25 November 2026 (with a record date of 26 November 2026) and will be paid on 18 December 2026.
  • Option for payment of the dividend in shares: shareholders will be able to elect to receive the balance of the dividend either in cash or in new Pernod Ricard shares, from 27 November to 11 December 2026 inclusive. The detailed terms and timetable are set out in Appendix 1 to this press release.
  • Renewal of Ms. Patricia Barbizet’s term of office as Director (her biography is set out in Appendix 2 to this press release).
  • Appointment of Mr. Johannes Huth as Director (his biography is set out in Appendix 2 to this press release).
  • Approval of, firstly, the components of the compensation paid or granted to Alexandre Ricard, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, for fiscal year 2025/26 and, secondly, the components of the compensation policy applicable to him for fiscal year 2026/27.

Following the Shareholders’ Meeting, the Board of Directors met and decided on the following changes to the composition of its Committees:

  • Renewal of Ms. Patricia Barbizet as Chair of the Nominations and Governance Committee, Chair of the CSR Committee and member of the Compensation Committee; and
  • Appointment of Mr. Albert Baladi as member of the Compensation Committee.

A summary table of the composition of the Board of Directors’ Committees following today’s Board of Directors’ meeting is set out in Appendix 3 to this press release.

The Shareholders’ Meeting was broadcast live and is available on replay, in French and English, on http://www.pernod-ricard.com.

APPENDIX 1 – PAYMENT OF THE SCRIP DIVIDEND

Timetable and terms of the option to receive the dividend in shares

The Shareholders’ Meeting approved, in particular, the option for shareholders to receive the entire undistributed dividend in cash or in newly issued shares (4th resolution of the Shareholders’ Meeting). Eligible Pernod Ricard shareholders will thus be able to receive the undistributed dividend, amounting to 2.35 euros per share (3rd resolution of the Shareholders’ Meeting), at their discretion, either in cash or in newly issued ordinary shares of Pernod Ricard. This measure is part of the Group's efforts to strengthen its financial discipline and balance sheet.

Terms of dividend payment

The issue price of the new shares to be delivered in payment of the dividend is 60.83 euros. This price corresponds to 90% of the average of the latest closing prices listed on the regulated Euronext Paris market during the 20 trading sessions preceding the date of the Shareholders’ Meeting, less the net amount of the undistributed dividend and rounded up to the next euro cent.

Shareholders must hold Pernod Ricard shares carrying dividend entitlement on the record date, namely Thursday, 26 November 2026.

The option to receive the dividend in new shares may be exercised by the shareholders between 27 November 2026 and 11 December 2026, inclusive, by submitting their request to the financial intermediaries authorised to pay the dividend or, for shareholders whose shares are directly registered in Pernod Ricard’s share accounts, to Société Générale Securities Services. After this date, the undistributed dividend will only be paid in cash.

The option to receive the dividend in new shares shall apply to the total amount of the undistributed dividend in respect of the shares each shareholder owns. If the amount of dividends in respect of which the option is exercised does not correspond to a whole number of shares, the shareholder may receive the next lower number of shares and receive the balance in cash.

The shares will be delivered on 18 December 2026 to shareholders who have elected to receive the dividend in shares (the dividend will be paid in cash on that same date to shareholders who have not elected to receive payment in shares). The shares so issued will carry immediate dividend rights and will therefore entitle the holder to any dividends decided upon from their date of issue.

The maximum number of new shares that may be issued to pay the undistributed dividend in shares is 9 730 289 shares, representing approximately 3.8 % of the total number of voting shares as of 19 November 2026.

New shares will be admitted to trading on Euronext Paris (ISIN Code: FR0000120693) as of 18 December 2026, on the same quotation line as the existing shares.

For any questions concerning the terms for payment of the dividend in shares, shareholders are advised to refer to the “Q&A” available on Pernod Ricard’s website (www.pernod-ricard.com).

Calendar for dividend payment

DATE

STAGE

Wednesday, 25 November 2026

Ex-dividend date: commencement of trading in Pernod Ricard shares ex-dividend.

Thursday, 26 November 2026

Record date: determination of shareholders’ holdings for the purpose of calculating the dividend amount.

From Friday, 27 November 2026 to Friday, 11 December 2026 inclusive

Election period during which eligible shareholders may elect to receive the dividend in shares. These dates may, however, vary depending on the financial intermediaries.

If no election is made, the undistributed dividend will be paid in cash.

Wednesday, 16 December 2026

Announcement of the results of the election for payment of the undistributed dividend.


Friday, 18 December 2026

Payment of the undistributed dividend:

  • For shareholders who have elected to receive payment in cash or have not made an election: payment of the dividend in cash.
  • For eligible shareholders who have elected to receive payment in shares within the election period: issuance and admission to trading of the new shares, and delivery to shareholders of the shares and any cash adjustment.

Disclaimer

This release constitutes the information document required under Article 1, paragraphs 4(h) and 5(g) of the Chapter I of the Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 June 2017, as amended. This release does not constitute an offer of securities requiring the approval of a prospectus.

Any shareholder considering electing to receive the dividend in shares is advised to consider the risks inherent in an investment in shares. For further information on Pernod Ricard, its business, strategy, financial results and the risks to which the Group is exposed, shareholders are advised to refer to the 2025/26 Universal Registration Document, available on Pernod Ricard’s website (www.pernod-ricard.com).

Each shareholder is responsible for ascertaining the legal, tax and regulatory conditions and consequences associated with exercising this option, having regard to their particular circumstances and the laws and regulations applicable to them. Where appropriate, shareholders are advised to consult a suitably qualified professional adviser on any legal, tax or regulatory matters. This option is available to shareholders resident in a Member State of the European Union or a State party to the Agreement on the European Economic Area (EEA) or in the United Kingdom. Shareholders resident outside those countries must independently ascertain and comply with any local restrictions and related conditions, and ascertain any consequences of exercising such an option, under applicable local law. The option to receive the dividend in shares is not available to shareholders resident in Australia, Japan or any other country in which such an option requires registration with, or authorisation from, the local securities regulatory authorities.

No offering document, prospectus or admission document has been or will be prepared or submitted to be approved by the Financial Conduct Authority (or any other authority) in relation to the payment of the dividend in shares. The offer of payment of the dividend in shares is intended to be made in the United Kingdom (“UK”) under the exemption from the prohibition on public offers of securities contained in Paragraph 8 of Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the UK Public Offers and Admissions to Trading Regulations 2024. This announcement and any other communication relating to the payment of the dividend in shares by Pernod Ricard are not being made, and such documents and/or materials have not been approved, by an authorised person for the purposes of Section 21 of the UK Financial Services and Markets Act 2000. In the UK, this announcement is only being distributed to, and is directed only at, and any offer subsequently made may only be directed at: (i) persons who are existing members or creditors of Pernod Ricard or other persons falling within Article 43 of the UK Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Financial Promotion) Order 2005, as amended, (ii) persons to whom this announcement may otherwise lawfully be communicated or caused to be communicated (all such persons together being referred to as “Relevant Persons”). This announcement must not be acted on or relied on in the UK by persons who are not Relevant Persons. In the UK, any investment or investment activity to which this announcement relates is only available to, and will be engaged in only with, Relevant Persons.

This document, together with any other document relating to the payment of the dividend in shares, may only be distributed in compliance with applicable laws and regulations. It does not constitute an offer to purchase or subscribe for securities, or a solicitation of any such offer, in any jurisdiction in which such an offer or solicitation would contravene applicable laws and regulations.

Furthermore, shareholders are reminded that, pursuant to Article 11, paragraph III, of Pernod Ricard’s Articles of Association, any individual or legal entity whose shareholding exceeds 0.5% of the share capital is required to notify Pernod Ricard of the total number of shares held by that individual or legal entity, by registered letter with acknowledgement of receipt, within four trading sessions of the date on which that threshold is exceeded. A further notification must be made on the same terms whenever any subsequent threshold in increments of 0.5% is crossed, up to and including the 4.5% threshold.

APPENDIX 2: BIOGRAPHIES OF THE DIRECTORS WHOSE RENEWAL OR APPOINTMENT WAS APPROVED BY THE SHAREHOLDERS’ MEETING OF 20 NOVEMBER 2026

Patricia Barbizet

Patricia Barbizet is a graduate of ESCP Europe and began her career in 1976 with the Renault Véhicules group in Treasury before becoming Finance Director of Renault Crédit International.

In 1989, she joined the Pinault Group as Chief Financial Officer and in 1992 she became Chief Executive Officer of Artémis, the Pinault family’s investment company, a position she held until 2018. From 2014 to 2016, she was also CEO & Chairwoman of Christie’s International and chaired the Investment Committee of Strategic Investment Fund (SIF) from 2008 to 2013. She is currently Chairwoman of Temaris & Associés, Chairwoman of Zoé SAS, and Director of Colombus.

Between April 2018 and July 2023, she held the position of Chairwoman of the Supervisory Board of Investissements d’Avenir France 2030. She was Chairwoman of the French High Committee on Corporate Governance (Haut Comité de Gouvernement d’Entreprise) from 2018 to 2023. She has been Chairwoman of AFEP since 1 July 2023.

Patricia Barbizet has been a Director of Pernod Ricard since 2018 and was appointed Lead Independent Director on 23 January 2019.

Johannes Huth

Johannes Huth, a German national, holds a B.Sc. from the London School of Economics and an MBA from the University of Chicago, and began his career at Salomon Brothers from 1986 to 1991, where he was Vice President in the mergers and acquisitions departments in London and New York.

data.title: Smithfield Foods Donates 40,000 Pounds of Protein During Mayflower Marathon
data.description:
SMITHFIELD, Va., Nov. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Smithfield Foods donated 40,000 pounds of protein to the 30th Annual Mayflower Marathon Holiday Food and Fund Drive to support the Virginia Peninsula Foodbank and Foodbank of Southeastern Virginia and the Eastern Shore.

“The holiday season reminds us how important it is to come together as a community,” said Jonathan Toms, senior community development manager for Smithfield Foods. “We’re grateful for the work our local foodbanks do throughout the year, and the Mayflower Marathon gives us another chance to support them and help put nutritious protein on the table for families in our area.”

The donated protein, including bacon, ham and sausage, will provide 160,000 servings for neighbors experiencing hunger in the greater Hampton Roads area.

“Many families across the Peninsula rely on the Foodbank and its partners to access higher-cost items like proteins,” said Bob Latvis, president and CEO of the Virginia Peninsula Foodbank. “Smithfield’s commitment to helping ensure that all of our neighbors are able to prepare nutritious, complete meals during the holiday season benefits our whole community.”

More than 25 local Smithfield employees supported the 57-hour event by collecting and organizing donations at the drop-off location in Hampton, Virginia.

“Increasing access to nutritious food is one of our top priorities at the Foodbank, and protein plays an important role in supporting the health and well-being of our neighbors,” said Christopher Tan, president and CEO of the Foodbank of Southeastern Virginia and the Eastern Shore. “Protein is also one of the most expensive foods for families to purchase and for foodbanks to provide. Smithfield's generosity helps us overcome that challenge and ensures more of our neighbors have access to the quality nutrition they need to thrive.”

Smithfield’s support for the Mayflower Marathon continues its long-standing commitment to addressing food insecurity and supporting the communities where its employees live and work.

Since 2008, Smithfield has donated more than 345 million servings of protein to fight hunger and address food insecurity through the company’s Helping Hungry Homes® program. To learn more about Smithfield’s initiatives to strengthen local communities, visit smithfieldfoods.com/good-is-what-we-do. 

About Smithfield Foods
Smithfield Foods, Inc. (Nasdaq: SFD) is an American food company with a leading position in packaged meats and fresh pork products. With a diverse brand portfolio and strong relationships with U.S. farmers and customers, we responsibly meet demand for quality protein around the world.

About Virginia Peninsula Foodbank  
Since 1986, Virginia Peninsula Foodbank has been a leader in local hunger relief by providing access to healthy foods across the nine cities and counties on the Peninsula. With the support of 120 partner agencies, the Foodbank has provided over 200 million meals to families facing hunger. It operates mobile food pantries throughout the month, provides emergency food assistance, prepares weekend bags of food and after-school meals for children, and advocates for our neighbors experiencing food and nutrition insecurity. The Foodbank also runs an accredited Culinary Training program, helping to address root causes of food insecurity and provide opportunities for students in financial hardship. The Foodbank is a proud partner of Feeding America, the Federation of Virginia Food Banks, and the United Way of the Virginia Peninsula. Our vision is to inspire hope by leading the effort for a hunger-free and properly nourished community. For more information, visit us online at our www.hrfoodbank.org.

About the Foodbank of Southeastern Virginia and the Eastern Shore 
Since 1981, the Foodbank of Southeastern Virginia and the Eastern Shore has provided more than 442 million meals to neighbors in need. As the region's largest hunger-relief organization, the Foodbank procures, stores, and distributes millions of pounds of food and other essential grocery products each year, serving 11 cities and counties through a network of 240+ partner agencies and 150 direct distributions. The Foodbank works to increase access to nutritious food for children, seniors, veterans, and families experiencing food insecurity, with fresh produce and lean protein accounting for nearly half of all food distributed. Through the support of dedicated staff, volunteers, donors, and community partners, the Foodbank is helping ensure more neighbors have consistent access to the food they need to live healthy, stable lives. Learn more at foodbankonline.org.

Sprocket Security Named a Leader in GigaOm Radar for Penetration Testing as a Service

Sprocket Security Named a Leader in GigaOm Radar for Penetration Testing as a Service

PR Newswire

MADISON, Wis., Nov. 20, 2026

One year after debuting as a Challenger and Outperformer, Sprocket earns perfect scores on four criteria as it pairs expert pentesters with a fleet of AI agents.

MADISON, Wis., Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sprocket Security has been named a Leader in the GigaOm Radar for Penetration Testing as a Service (PTaaS) v5. Sprocket placed as a Leader in the report's Agile Optimizers scorecards and earned perfect marks on test launch efficiency, attack surface integration, rules of engagement controls, and the testing audit trail.

 Sprocket Security has been named a Leader in the GigaOm Radar for Penetration Testing as a Service (PTaaS) v5.

The placement marks a clear step up from 2025, when GigaOm recognized Sprocket as a Challenger and Outperformer. In the year between, Sprocket expanded its capabilities with a fleet of AI agents that work alongside its pentesters, extending how much of the attack surface gets tested and how quickly.

From Challenger to Leader

This year's report, authored by GigaOm analyst Chris Ray, maps four buyer profiles to four quadrants. It frames five market themes around the questions buyers should ask before signing: who performs the test, how it reaches internal networks, and what evidence an auditor will accept?

"Sprocket Security earns its Leader position by pairing AI testing agents with human validation of every finding, and wrapping both in machine-enforced scope, a customer kill switch and a checksummed audit trail, so its testing keeps pace with a changing attack surface without giving up control," Ray shared.

Sprocket's top scores reflect how the platform runs day to day:

Test launch efficiency (5.0): Teams scope and start testing without weeks of kickoff calls and paperwork.

Attack surface integration (5.0): Testing follows the attack surface as it changes, so new assets get tested as they appear.

Rules of engagement controls (5.0): Customers set what gets tested, when, and how, with guardrails built into the platform.

Testing audit trail (5.0): Every action is logged, giving security teams and auditors a record of what was tested and what was found.

Expert Pentesters, Now With an AI Fleet

Sprocket was founded because point-in-time pentests couldn't keep up with how companies change. Continuous testing closed part of that gap. Sprocket's AI agents close more of it, running alongside its pentesters on the Sprocket platform:

Apex: an agentic pentester for unauthenticated web applications, mapping each app and testing its own theories about where it might break.

Link: an agentic pentester for authenticated web applications, testing what sits behind the login.

Pinion: an agentic pentester for internal networks, falling the attack paths worth chasing.

Sprocket's pentesters direct the work and validate what the agents find, so customers get more coverage without trading away the judgment of an experienced tester.

"A year ago GigaOm called us a Challenger. Today we are a Leader, and agentic innovation is why. We put a fleet of AI agents to work next to our pentesters for all types of testing, and the results show up in these scores," said Casey Cammilleri, CEO and founder of Sprocket Security. "Buyers are asking who is actually testing, whether it reaches the parts of the network attackers go after, and whether the results will hold up with an auditor. Our answer is experienced pentesters with agents that extend their reach, on a platform that shows its work."

What Customers Can Expect

Organizations that work with Sprocket Security get:

  • Continuous pentesting that follows the attack surface as it grows, not a once-a-year snapshot.
  • Offensive security experts with deep experience across cloud, infrastructure, and application security.
  • AI agents that extend testing coverage, supervised and validated by those experts.
  • Clear rules of engagement controls and a full audit trail for every test.
  • Remediation guidance and retesting to confirm issues are fixed.

Looking Forward

Sprocket will keep expanding its AI fleet and testing coverage. Every new agent is held to Sprocket's Safety Framework for Autonomous Offensive Security Agents, which requires agents to stay within scope, stop at proof, log every action, and let humans step in at any point. The aim is to give buyers clear answers to the questions GigaOm says to ask: who is testing, how far the testing reaches, and what evidence it leaves behind.

Security leaders can access a complimentary copy of the GigaOm Radar for Penetration Testing as a Service v5 at https://www.sprocketsecurity.com/gigaom.

About Sprocket Security

Sprocket Security provides a technology-powered continuous penetration testing platform. Named in GigaOm and Gartner reports this year, Sprocket continuously monitors customer environments and triggers hybrid testing based on each customer's dynamic attack surface and emerging threats. Unlike legacy penetration testing, Sprocket's continuous approach delivers real-time insights and adaptive security, giving organizations a security posture that reflects today, not their last test.

data.title: My husband spent $80,000 on a boat, yet says my plans for a $100,000 pottery studio are irresponsible. Who's right?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'We have $2.9 million in retirement accounts. That includes some money that we inherited about 10 years ago.'

"My husband, however, is skeptical. He says that's a lot of money to spend on something that I'm trying to profit from." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

My husband and I have been married for 31 years. He's 65 and I'm 62. I work part-time in a dental office and we have a house that's fully paid off. It's worth about $900,000. Best of all, we have $2.9 million in retirement accounts. That includes some money that we inherited about 10 years ago.

For the last 15 years, I have dreamed of opening my own pottery studio. I've taken lessons at our Saturday market for several years, and I find it extremely meditative and also a wonderful pastime. There's a space near an old rail depot, about 900 square feet, which would be perfect for a pottery studio, where I could teach others. By my estimations, insurance, equipment and rent would require about $100,000.

My husband, however, is skeptical. He says that's a lot of money to spend on something that I'm trying to profit from. My sister says it's bad timing given that we're both heading into retirement. Three years ago, he purchased a boat for $80,000 and spent $12,000 on a new motor and fishfinder. He barely used it, and finally sold it at a loss.

I'm not claiming my pottery studio will make us rich, but I'm perfectly willing to come up with a business plan and set a budget, with a red line on the amount of money I would be prepared to lose. I'd actually also start a lot smaller and build up if the price is right. We could have 30 years ahead of us in retirement, and I want to spend it doing something that brings me a lot of joy.

Am I being unrealistic?

A 62-Year-Old Wife

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'I like the idea of a big return': My financial adviser wants me to invest $350,000 in a UAE data center. Is this risky?

Tell your husband that you're not giving up before you've even started.

Dear Wife,

From your letter, it doesn't sound like pottery is just a business for you.

For you, pottery is a passion, and it's important to have something you like doing in retirement. If you are going to choose to open a business, it should be something you will love because it won't always be easy, and you may need to rely on that bedrock of belief when the going gets tough. That's in addition to financial projections, advice from an accountant, knowing where you draw a hard line on the budget if sales dry up, and even a Plan B for the space.

I'm not going to tell you to open a business and spend $100,000, which could be a little on the high side, although you will know more when you compare this plan to similar-sized businesses and complete your due diligence. More important, I'm not going to tell you not to do it, and I don't think anyone else should, either, at least not without hearing you out, visiting the proposed site and, crucially, seeing your business plan. What stands out from your letter is your husband's immediate, possibly knee-jerk, opposition.

However, pointing out that he bought an $80,000 motorboat and ended up throwing good money after bad and selling it at a loss may be fair, but it doesn't help your cause. Yes, he decided to pursue something that he eventually tired of or decided wasn't worth all the hassle and expense. He's the one who apparently lost interest in a project after spending nearly six figures, not you. But it won't help to trade successes and failures in a tit-for-tat argument.

If a pottery studio is a vocation, you have earned the right to at least look into it.

It may be that you don't have to lease this building, as romantic as it sounds. You could rent a space at a retirement center or local school, at least initially, invest in the equipment to host pottery classes, build up word of mouth or an online presence and see how much demand is out there. That way, you won't be locked into a lease if the demand is not there. It will also help you envision what success means to you. Is it teaching a twice-weekly class? Or running a full-time studio?

You raise a great point when you say your retirement is not about doing nothing, or spending all of your time on the golf course or tennis court, or sitting in your garden reading - rather, it's about pursuing work that fulfills you. If pottery is a vocation for you, you have earned the right to at least look into it, given that you have worked for probably 40-plus years in jobs that helped you and your husband build a $2.9 million nest egg, even if those jobs were not your first choice.

For what it's worth, your business plan should include projected costs, including the lease, insurance, equipment, advertising, branding and marketing; projected revenue; the target market (there may be schools or senior centers nearby that would jump at the opportunity for their community to learn pottery); and, of course, the competition (find out if there are similar businesses in your area and, if so, how close they are and what they charge for classes).

Related: 'I don't want to die on the sales floor': I'm 67 and earn $19.50 an hour at a big-box store. When can I finally retire?

Running the numbers

You won't win this argument on statements that your husband is the proverbial pot calling the kettle black, and you may not "win" the argument at all. But you will lend more credence to your pottery studio idea through data. You have $2.9 million for retirement, a mortgage-free house worth $900,000, hardly any debt, a husband who has already retired, Social Security coming down the pike, and you continue to work part-time, although that may have to end if you set up this studio.

To put your small business in context: Startup costs of $100,000 represent 3.45% of your retirement account balance. That's not nothing, but neither is it an outrageous, extravagant risk, particularly given that this is an investment to further a pastime that brings you joy and, hopefully, makes money. What is your annual income now? What will it be in five years? What are your annual expenses? How much of your retirement is in traditional accounts versus Roth?

Another missing piece of this puzzle: Do you have a "fun money" account, an emergency fund or CDs or bonds to draw from? Otherwise, you would have to take this money from your investments. That would mean you need to take more than $100,000, because you would have to pay tax on the money you withdraw from a traditional IRA or 401(k). You would lose future investment returns (which you would ideally recoup, even if only in part, from your studio).

A $100,000 startup cost represents 3.45% of your retirement-account balance.

Tell your husband that you're not giving up before you've even started, just as you would not expect him to give up on a passion project without at least stress-testing the finances. The unspoken part of this conversation, particularly after his motorboat project, is hanging over you. It does not sound like you are asking him for permission, per se - rather, you are requesting his support, and I assume you have both contributed to your retirement fund, either as a corporate worker or a homemaker.

Agree on a maximum amount you can afford to lose on a studio. You will need working capital, particularly in the early stages, when you are building your reputation. This is an opportunity to step back and ask what you want from retirement. How do you want to spend your savings? What kind of issues require unanimous agreement? (Did you agree to the motorboat purchase, for instance?) How will you navigate such issues while respecting each other's space?

A woman named Kyla Glendenning opened up a pottery studio in Fort Lauderdale and said she had revenue of $71,000 in the first six months, but spent nearly $20,000 on Facebook advertisements. That tells me, in addition to the costs of setting up a studio, signing a lease and buying equipment, that your biggest challenges will be getting the word out that you exist. Her online tutorials and videos on social media - where I found her - also require both time and money.

Don't let anyone crack your bowls before they've even hit the kiln.

Related: My wife says we can't afford to retire. I vetoed her $8,000 trip to Italy. We're in our 60s and have $4 million. Do I keep working?

data.title: Medicare beneficiaries could skip the nursing home for cheaper care at home under new bill
data.description:
By Jessica Hall

The plan would free up hospital and nursing-home beds - and lower costs

Care at home could help cut costs, make patients more comfortable and free up much-needed hospital and nursing-home beds, proponents of the bill said.

A new bipartisan bill would create a five-year pilot program for Medicare beneficiaries to receive nursing care and intensive rehabilitation services in their home rather than in a nursing facility.

After a hospital stay, Medicare beneficiaries who need additional care often get transferred on a short-term basis to nursing homes for rehabilitation. The new proposal would allow those patients to get a higher level of nursing care at home, with the goal of freeing up hospital and nursing-home beds, lowering costs and keeping patients more comfortable in their own homes. The bill, called the Bringing Rehabilitation, Integrated Delivery, and Greater Extended Care at Home Act, was introduced by Rep. Adrian Smith, a Nebraska Republican, and Rep. Debbie Dingell, a Democrat from Michigan.

"When it comes to healthcare, one size does not fit all, and patients deserve to have choices. Too often, options are unnecessarily restricted - especially for Medicare beneficiaries," Smith said in a press statement.

The bill also calls for a study to be conducted comparing the quality, outcomes and costs of home care versus facility-based care.

"Most patients prefer to receive care at home, so we must do more to support access to skilled nursing care in the home for patients who prefer that option. And most importantly, it is the less expensive option for both families and the government," Dingell said in a press statement.

The proposal comes as Americans are living longer but not always remaining in good health. There's a difference of about 12 years between a person's lifespan and their so-called healthspan - the number of years they are healthy - according to research from Age Wave, a think tank and consultancy focused on aging and longevity.

If people are living longer with disease and disability, obtaining care and finding caregivers will become more of an issue. As many as 77% of people ages 50 and older want to remain in their own home as they age, according to AARP. Nursing homes, meanwhile, are facing financial pressures and staffing shortages, with hundreds having closed since the COVID-19 pandemic, especially in rural areas. A JAMA Internal Medicine study found that national nursing home capacity dropped 5% from 2019 to 2024.

"Seniors deserve to be able to receive timely, safe, and high-quality care after a hospital stay. Whether this can be achieved in the home on a national scale is something that requires thoughtful consideration - especially given that our nation is aging and caregiver shortages are growing across health care," Dan Ciolek, associate vice president of therapy advocacy for the American Health Care Association/National Center for Assisted Living, the industry trade group for nursing homes and assisted-living facilities, said in an email to MarketWatch. "We look forward to working with Congress on viable, innovative solutions to ensure that seniors get the care they need in the setting best suited to them."

The proposal follows another Medicare pilot program called Acute Hospital Care at Home that received a five-year extension earlier this year. Under that program, Medicare beneficiaries can get hospital-level care for conditions such as acute infection, heart failure or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in their own home.

"Hospital at home demonstrated that seniors can be treated at home safely and effectively. The BRIDGE Care at Home Act would test the idea of skilled nursing and intensive rehabilitation services at home, helping patients maintain their independence, supporting caregivers and giving providers an alternative to working in an institutional setting," Krista Drobac, the founder of Moving Health Home, a coalition of healthcare organizations that advocates for home-based care, said in a press statement.

Getting skilled-nursing rehabilitation in the home would allow "patients to rebuild functional independence directly in the spaces where they actually live. Patients sleep better, move more and face lower risks of delirium and ... complications when their acute recovery happens at home," Swetha Gudibanda, medical director of Sanford Health Marshfield Clinic Home Recovery Care in Marshfield, Wis., said in statement in support of the BRIDGE proposal.

-Jessica Hall
